chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 4 — From Cain to Noah
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest primary-language witnesses responsibly available for this chapter. The surviving Hebrew text of 11Q12 (11QJubilees) was used for Jubilees 4:6–11, 4:13–14, 4:16–17, and 4:29–31 wherever its fragmentary lines preserve wording. The complete chapter and every physical gap follow the Ethiopic (Geʽez) text preserved in manuscripts A–D and printed on text pages 14–18 of R. H. Charles’s 1895 critical edition, The Ethiopic Version of the Hebrew Book of Jubilees. No modern English translation was used as the translation base, no commentary was used as Scripture, and no wording absent from the primary witnesses was supplied.

verses.text: In the third week of the second jubilee, Eve gave birth to Cain; in the fourth week she gave birth to Abel; and in the fifth week she gave birth to her daughter Awan.
verses.study: The genealogy is placed within the book’s measured calendar. Human life continues beyond Eden through births that will lead both to violence and to a preserved family line.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:1–2 — Eve bears Cain and Abel outside Eden
Genesis 5:1–2 — Adam’s family is recorded as a continuing human line

verses.text: In the first year of the third jubilee, Cain killed Abel because Abel’s sacrifice was accepted, but Cain’s offering was not accepted.
verses.study: Cain answers rejected worship by attacking the brother whose gift was received. The text locates murder in jealousy that refuses correction.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:3–5 — God regards Abel and his offering but not Cain and his offering
1 John 3:12 — Cain kills his brother because his own deeds are evil

verses.text: He killed him in the field, and Abel’s blood cried out from the ground to heaven, accusing Cain because he had killed him.
verses.study: Hidden violence becomes a public accusation before heaven. The earth itself bears witness to innocent blood.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:8–10 — Abel is killed in the field and his blood cries from the ground
Hebrews 12:24 — Abel’s blood is recalled as speaking

verses.text: The Lord rebuked Cain because he had killed Abel. Because of his brother’s blood, God made him a wanderer on the earth and cursed him from the ground.
verses.study: The judgment fits Cain’s act: blood shed upon the ground disrupts his relation to the ground. His violence produces exile and instability.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:11–12 — Cain is cursed from the ground and becomes a restless wanderer
Numbers 35:33 — shed blood pollutes the land

verses.text: For this reason it is written on the heavenly tablets: ‘Cursed is anyone who strikes his neighbor with malice.’ Let everyone who sees or hears say, ‘Amen.’ Anyone who sees it and does not report it will be cursed like the offender.
verses.study: The chapter extends responsibility beyond the murderer to truthful witnesses. Silence that protects violence becomes participation in its concealment.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 27:24 — a curse is pronounced on one who strikes a neighbor in secret
Leviticus 5:1 — a witness bears guilt when withholding known testimony

verses.text: Therefore, whenever we come before the Lord our God, we report every sin committed in heaven or on earth, in light or in darkness, and in every place.
verses.study: No setting hides wrongdoing from heavenly accountability. The angelic speakers portray judgment as informed by complete testimony.
crossReferences: Ecclesiastes 12:14 — God brings every deed into judgment, including hidden things
Psalm 139:11–12 — darkness is not dark before God

verses.text: Adam and his wife mourned Abel for four weeks of years. In the fourth year of the fifth week they rejoiced, and Adam again knew his wife. She bore him a son, and he named him Seth, saying, ‘The Lord has appointed another offspring for us on the earth in place of Abel, because Cain killed him.’
verses.study: Long mourning gives way to renewed life. Seth does not erase Abel’s death, but his birth preserves hope for the family.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:25 — Eve receives Seth as another offspring in place of Abel
Genesis 5:3 — Adam fathers Seth in his likeness

verses.text: In the sixth week Adam fathered his daughter Azura.
verses.study: The brief notice supplies the next generation within the chapter’s family record. Each life is placed in ordered time.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:4 — Adam fathers other sons and daughters
Acts 17:26 — humanity’s generations and appointed times stand under God

verses.text: Cain took his sister Awan as his wife, and at the end of the fourth jubilee she bore him Enoch. In the first year of the first week of the fifth jubilee, houses were built on the earth. Cain built a city and named it after his son Enoch.
verses.study: Cain’s family develops settled life and builds the first named city. The achievement remains marked by Cain’s attempt to establish permanence after being sentenced to wander.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:17 — Cain builds a city and names it after his son Enoch
Psalm 49:11 — people name lands after themselves while seeking permanence

verses.text: Adam again knew his wife Eve, and she bore nine more children.
verses.study: The family expands beyond the few named descendants. The record emphasizes continued fruitfulness after death entered human experience.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:4 — Adam has other sons and daughters
Genesis 1:28 — humanity receives the command to be fruitful and multiply

verses.text: In the fifth week of the fifth jubilee, Seth took his sister Azura as his wife. In the fourth year of the sixth week she bore him Enosh.
verses.study: Seth’s line advances through another carefully dated birth. Enosh will become associated with public invocation of the Lord.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:26 — Seth fathers Enosh
Genesis 5:6 — the genealogy continues from Seth to Enosh

verses.text: He was the first to call upon the name of the Lord on the earth.
verses.study: The text marks a new beginning in worship: the Lord’s name is openly invoked within the growing human family.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:26 — people begin to call upon the name of the Lord
Psalm 116:4 — the worshiper calls upon the Lord’s name for deliverance

verses.text: In the seventh jubilee, during the third week, Enosh took his sister Noam as his wife. In the third year of the fifth week she bore him a son, and he named him Kenan.
verses.study: The genealogy continues without losing the calendar’s structure. The chapter presents history as a sequence known and recorded before God.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:9 — Enosh fathers Kenan
1 Chronicles 1:2 — Kenan stands in the line from Adam

verses.text: At the end of the eighth jubilee, Kenan took his sister Mualeleth as his wife. In the ninth jubilee, in the third year of its first week, she bore him a son, and he named him Mahalalel.
verses.study: Another generation is joined to the measured chronology. The repeated pattern links family continuity with ordered time.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:12 — Kenan fathers Mahalalel
Luke 3:37–38 — the genealogy traces this line back through Kenan to Adam

verses.text: In the second week of the tenth jubilee, Mahalalel took Dinah as his wife. She was the daughter of Barakiel, his father’s brother. In the sixth year of the third week she bore him a son, and he named him Jared, because in his days the angels of the Lord called Watchers descended to the earth to teach humanity’s children and to establish justice and righteousness upon the earth.
verses.study: Jared’s name is tied to descent, introducing the Watchers’ original commission. Their assigned purpose is instruction in justice, which makes their later corruption a betrayal of their calling.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:15 — Mahalalel fathers Jared
Daniel 4:13 — a heavenly being is called a watcher and a holy one
Genesis 18:19 — instruction is directed toward righteousness and justice

verses.text: In the eleventh jubilee Jared took Baraka as his wife; she was the daughter of Rasujal, his father’s brother. In the fourth week of that jubilee she became his wife, and in the fourth year of the fifth week she bore him a son, and he named him Enoch.
verses.study: Enoch enters the genealogy through another precisely located birth. His life will interrupt the chapter’s ordinary pattern of descent and death.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:18 — Jared fathers Enoch
Jude 14 — Enoch is identified as the seventh from Adam

verses.text: Enoch was the first among those born on earth to learn writing, instruction, and wisdom. He wrote in a book the signs of heaven according to the order of their months, so that humanity’s children might know the seasons of the years according to the order of each month.
verses.study: Knowledge is received, ordered, and written for others. Enoch’s attention to the heavens serves faithful understanding of appointed times.
crossReferences: Genesis 1:14 — heavenly lights mark signs, seasons, days, and years
Sirach 44:16 — Enoch is remembered as an example of knowledge and faithfulness

verses.text: He was the first to write a testimony and testify to humanity’s children among the generations of the earth. He recounted the weeks of the jubilees, made known the days of the years, arranged the months in order, and recounted the sabbaths of the years, just as we had made them known to him.
verses.study: Enoch’s written testimony joins chronology with moral witness. Revelation is preserved so later generations can remember both sacred time and accountability.
crossReferences: Habakkuk 2:2 — revelation is written clearly for those who read it
Deuteronomy 31:19 — a written witness is preserved for later generations

verses.text: In a vision during sleep he saw what had been and what would be—what would happen to humanity’s children throughout their generations until the day of judgment. He saw and understood everything, wrote his testimony, and placed it on the earth for all humanity’s children and their generations.
verses.study: Enoch’s vision spans history toward judgment. Writing makes the warning available beyond the seer’s own lifetime.
crossReferences: Daniel 7:1 — a night vision is written down as a record
Jude 14–15 — Enoch’s testimony announces coming judgment

verses.text: In the twelfth jubilee, during its seventh week, Enoch took Edna as his wife. She was the daughter of Danel, his father’s brother. In the sixth year of that week she bore him a son, and he named him Methuselah.
verses.study: The visionary remains within ordinary family life and passes the ancestral line forward. Revelation and household responsibility appear together.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:21 — Enoch fathers Methuselah
Genesis 5:22 — Enoch walks with God while continuing family life

verses.text: Afterward Enoch was with the angels of God for six jubilees of years. They showed him everything on earth and in the heavens, including the dominion of the sun, and he wrote it all down.
verses.study: Enoch’s heavenly instruction expands from calendar signs to the ordered realms of creation. His task is to receive and preserve what is shown.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:22–24 — Enoch walks with God and is taken by God
1 Enoch 72:1 — Enoch records the courses of the heavenly lights

verses.text: He also testified against the Watchers who had sinned with the daughters of men. They had begun to join themselves to the daughters of men and defile themselves, and Enoch testified against them all.
verses.study: Those commissioned to teach righteousness become defendants before the testimony they violated. Greater knowledge does not shield rebellion from judgment.
crossReferences: Genesis 6:1–4 — heavenly beings take women from the daughters of humanity
1 Enoch 12:3–6 — Enoch is sent to announce judgment to the Watchers
2 Peter 2:4 — sinning angels are kept for judgment

verses.text: He was taken from among humanity’s children, and we led him into the garden of Eden in majesty and honor. There he writes the condemnation and judgment of the world and all the wickedness of humanity’s children.
verses.study: Enoch’s removal does not end his witness. In the text’s portrayal, he continues as a heavenly scribe whose record exposes human wickedness.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:24 — God takes Enoch so that he is no longer among humanity
Malachi 3:16 — a record is written before the Lord
Revelation 20:12 — written records stand open at judgment

verses.text: Because of these deeds, the waters of the flood came over all the land of Eden. Enoch was appointed there as a sign and as a witness against all humanity’s children, so that he might recount every deed of the generations until the day of condemnation.
verses.study: The flood is presented as judgment on accumulated corruption. Enoch’s continuing testimony links deeds across generations with their final accounting.
crossReferences: Genesis 6:5–7 — pervasive human wickedness leads to the flood decree
Matthew 24:37–39 — the days of Noah become a sign of coming judgment

verses.text: He burned the sanctuary’s incense—sweet spices acceptable before the Lord—on the mountain of the south.
verses.study: Enoch’s service includes priestly worship as well as written testimony. Fragrant incense represents an offering accepted in God’s presence.
crossReferences: Exodus 30:34–38 — sacred incense is made from fragrant spices for the Lord
Psalm 141:2 — prayer rises before God like incense

verses.text: For the Lord has four places on the earth: the garden of Eden, the mountain of the east, this mountain where you are today—Mount Sinai—and Mount Zion, which will be sanctified in the new creation for the sanctification of the earth. Through it the earth will be sanctified from all its guilt and impurity throughout the generations of the world.
verses.study: The four places connect creation, revelation, worship, and promised renewal. Zion’s future sanctification points from a defiled earth toward a cleansed creation.
crossReferences: Exodus 19:20 — the Lord descends upon Mount Sinai
Psalm 132:13–14 — the Lord chooses Zion as his dwelling
Isaiah 65:17–19 — new creation and joy are centered on renewed Jerusalem

verses.text: In the fourteenth jubilee, in the first year of the third week, Methuselah took Edna as his wife. She was the daughter of Azrial, his father’s brother. She bore him a son, and he named him Lamech.
verses.study: The genealogy resumes after the account of Enoch’s exceptional life. The line continues toward Noah despite the corruption already announced.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:25 — Methuselah fathers Lamech
1 Chronicles 1:3 — Methuselah and Lamech stand in the line leading to Noah

verses.text: In the fifteenth jubilee, during the third week, Lamech took a wife named Betenos, the daughter of Barakiel, his father’s brother. During that week she bore him a son, and he named him Noah, saying, ‘This one will comfort me from my distress, from all my labor, and from the ground that the Lord cursed.’
verses.study: Noah’s name carries hope for relief within a world burdened by cursed ground. Lamech longs for comfort, though the coming story will first pass through judgment.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:28–29 — Lamech names Noah in hope of comfort from toil and cursed ground
Genesis 3:17–19 — the cursed ground makes human labor painful

verses.text: At the end of the nineteenth jubilee, in the sixth year of its seventh week, Adam died. All his children buried him in the land where he had been created, and he was the first to be buried in the earth.
verses.study: Adam returns to the ground from which he was formed. The first human burial confirms the mortality announced after transgression.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:5 — Adam dies at nine hundred thirty years
Genesis 3:19 — the human formed from dust returns to dust

verses.text: He fell seventy years short of one thousand years, for one thousand years are like one day in the testimony of heaven. Therefore it was written concerning the tree of knowledge, ‘On the day you eat from it, you will die.’ For this reason Adam did not complete the years of that day, because he died within it.
verses.study: The chapter interprets Adam’s lifespan through heaven’s measure of a day. The warning in Eden is therefore fulfilled within the larger divine reckoning of time.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:17 — death is warned for the day of eating
Psalm 90:4 — a thousand years before God are like a passing day
2 Peter 3:8 — one day with the Lord is like a thousand years

verses.text: At the end of that jubilee, Cain was killed after Adam in the same year. His house fell upon him, and he died inside it, killed by its stones. He had killed Abel with a stone, and by a stone he was killed in righteous judgment.
verses.study: Cain’s death mirrors the means of Abel’s murder. The narrative presents his end as measured justice rather than accidental misfortune.
crossReferences: Genesis 9:6 — the shedding of human blood brings judgment
Obadiah 15 — a person’s deed returns upon his own head

verses.text: For this reason it was established on the heavenly tablets: ‘With the instrument by which a man kills his neighbor, by that same instrument he will be killed. As he wounded the other, so it will be done to him.’
verses.study: The ruling expresses proportionate judgment: violence is answered according to its own measure. Human life may not be treated as disposable.
crossReferences: Leviticus 24:19–20 — injury is repaid according to the injury inflicted
Matthew 26:52 — those who take the sword perish by the sword

verses.text: In the twenty-fifth jubilee, in the first year of the fifth week, Noah took Emzara as his wife. She was the daughter of Rakeel, his father’s brother. In the third year of that week she bore him Shem; in its fifth year she bore him Ham; and in the first year of the sixth week she bore him Japheth.
verses.study: The chapter closes with the sons through whom humanity will continue beyond the flood. The genealogy reaches the threshold of the coming judgment and preservation.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:32 — Noah fathers Shem, Ham, and Japheth
Genesis 9:18–19 — the earth is repopulated through Noah’s three sons

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 4 traces humanity from Cain and Abel to Noah within the book’s jubilee calendar. Cain’s murder is not hidden: Abel’s blood cries from the earth, heaven receives testimony, and the heavenly tablets condemn both malicious violence and the witness who conceals it. The births of Seth and later generations show that life continues without minimizing the loss.

The genealogy leads to Enoch, whose life joins wisdom, writing, sacred chronology, prophecy, and worship. He records the signs of heaven and the measured times of years, bears testimony to later generations, and speaks against the Watchers when they abandon their commission to teach justice. Knowledge carries responsibility; those who violate what they know face judgment.

Enoch’s removal to Eden makes him a continuing witness in the chapter’s account. Eden, the mountain of the east, Sinai, and Zion form a geography of holiness extending from creation through revelation to new creation. Zion’s promised sanctification looks toward an earth cleansed of guilt and impurity.

The closing generations hold judgment and hope together. Adam returns to the earth, Cain dies by the same kind of instrument he used against Abel, and proportionate justice is written as a lasting principle. Yet the family line reaches Noah and his sons, preparing for both the flood and the preservation that follows it.

crossReferences: Genesis 4:1–26 — Cain kills Abel, receives judgment, and the lines of Cain and Seth begin
Genesis 5:1–32 — the genealogy runs from Adam through Enoch to Noah and his sons
Genesis 6:1–8 — heavenly rebellion and human corruption precede the flood
Leviticus 24:17–22 — proportionate justice protects human life
Psalm 90:1–4 — divine time exceeds human lifespans
Isaiah 65:17–19 — new creation brings renewed holiness and joy
Daniel 4:13, 17 — heavenly Watchers participate in divine judgment
Hebrews 11:4–5 — Abel’s faithful offering and Enoch’s removal are remembered
Jude 14–15 — Enoch testifies concerning judgment
Revelation 20:11–12 — the dead are judged according to recorded deeds
